opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a common misconception about what RL environments are for. People sometimes look at them and say, "Oh, you're just teaching the model to do this specific task, you're training it on the test." And I don't think that's really the right way to think about it.

The way I think about it is that the purpose isn't to teach the model every individual skill one by one. It's a bit like pre-training. In pre-training we didn't set out to teach the model each fact or each pattern; we gave it an enormous, diverse distribution of data, and what emerged was generalization. Abilities showed up that nobody explicitly trained for. RL environments are the same kind of bet, just in a different regime. You build a wide range of tasks: coding, math, using tools, operating a computer, long-horizon agentic work. The hope, and increasingly what we actually observe, is that the model learns something more general: how to plan, how to check its own work, how to recover when something goes wrong, how to persist on a hard problem.

So the individual environment matters less than the breadth. Early on, with GPT-1 and GPT-2 era models, you trained on narrow datasets and got narrow capabilities. Then you trained on a broad scrape of the internet and suddenly things generalized. I think we're somewhere along that same curve with RL. Each environment is a sample from the space of things we want models to be able to do, and as you add more and more of them, the generalization gets better.

There's also a practical side to it. Pre-training gives you a model that knows a lot, but knowing isn't the same as doing. RL environments are where the model learns to act: to take a sequence of steps toward a goal and get feedback on whether it got there. That's really the bridge from a very knowledgeable system to something that can do real work, the kind of thing a junior engineer or a researcher does over hours or days.

And I'd add one caveat. Because you're optimizing against a reward, you have to be careful. Models can find shortcuts, reward hacking, ways of satisfying the letter of the task without the spirit. So a lot of the craft is in designing environments that are robust and actually reward the behavior you want. That's both a capabilities question and a safety question, and I think the two are pretty intertwined there.

r001.rationale: The response says broad RL environments are intended to help models learn general abilities such as planning and self-checking, including capabilities nobody explicitly trained for.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that RL environments are really the mechanism by which you decide what you want the model to be good at. In the pre-training era, the question was mostly "how much data can we get and how much compute can we throw at it," and the data was just sort of whatever was out there. With RL, you're constructing the task. You're saying, here's a thing I want the model to be able to do, here's how I'm going to tell whether it did it well, and then you let the model grind against that.

So the purpose, at the most basic level, is to turn capabilities you care about into something that's actually trainable. If I want a model that can write a working piece of software, or carry a long agentic task through to completion, or reason carefully about a hard scientific question, I need a setting where it can try, fail, get a signal, and try again. The environment is where that happens.

But I'd say there's a second purpose that people underrate, which is that environments are also where you shape behavior, not just capability. The model learns what you reward. If your environment only rewards getting the answer, you'll get a model that's willing to cut corners, game the checker, do whatever it takes. If the environment also captures things like honesty, following the spirit of the instructions, not taking actions the user didn't ask for, then you're training that in too. So from our perspective, environment design is a safety lever as much as a capability lever. The two are really the same problem looked at from different angles.

And then the practical reality is that this is hard. The bottleneck has shifted. It used to be compute and data in the loose sense. Now a huge amount of the work is, can you build enough high-quality, diverse, hard-to-game environments that actually reflect the real tasks people want done? That's a lot of very careful, fairly unglamorous engineering, and I think it's where a lot of the progress over the next couple of years is going to come from.

r001.rationale: The response says environments make desired capabilities trainable and should be diverse, but it does not state that training across many environments enables generalization to skills that were not explicitly trained.

astra-6.text:
I think the purpose is to give the model a way to learn from trying things and seeing whether they work. In pretraining, you learn from this enormous collection of things humans have written. That’s incredibly powerful, but it’s different from being able to take an action, observe the consequences, and improve your strategy.

Programming is a good example. You can write some code, run it, get an error, and try to fix it. The environment gives you feedback that isn’t just someone saying, “That looks like a good answer.” There’s some external test of whether you accomplished the task.

The important question is whether the environments teach something general. You don’t want a model that’s merely very good at the particular exercises you constructed. You want it to learn how to investigate a problem, recover from mistakes, and carry out a longer sequence of actions. So I’d think of environments as a means to develop those capabilities, with the real test being whether they transfer to situations the model hasn’t encountered before.

r001.rationale: It says environments should develop general capabilities that transfer to situations the model has not encountered before, beyond the specific exercises used in training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the purpose is to give the model a way to try things, get feedback, and improve at tasks where you can tell whether it succeeded. With pretraining, you’re learning from what people have already written down. With reinforcement learning, the model can actually work through a problem and discover which approaches work.

The hard question is what transfers. You don’t ultimately want a model that’s very good at your particular training environment. You want it to learn things like how to recover from a mistake, how to check its work, or how to pursue a goal over many steps. So I’d think about environments as a means of teaching those more general capabilities. The score in the environment is useful insofar as it tells you something about that broader learning.

r001.rationale: The response says environments should teach capabilities that transfer beyond a particular training environment, such as recovering from mistakes, checking work, and pursuing goals over many steps.
